title: Tennessee Stops an Execution and Orders a Review
summary:
The death penalty is a punishment for very serious crimes. Tennessee planned to carry out this punishment on Wednesday night for a woman named Christa Pike. She is 50 years old. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. Both of them were teenagers in Knoxville at the time.

The execution was set for the morning, but a court order stopped it for about nine hours. Then the U.S. Supreme Court gave officials the go-ahead.

At night, the state gave Pike two doses of a drug called pentobarbital. Catherine Sweeney, a WPLN reporter who was a media witness, and others said Pike was still talking after the first dose. After the second dose, she was heard breathing for more than 20 minutes. The state then stopped the attempt. Officials later confirmed that Pike was taken by ambulance to a medical facility.

The Tennessee Department of Correction says its team "followed every step in the protocol." It is also standing by the drug it uses. Governor Bill Lee has ordered a third-party review. He also canceled the other execution that was planned for later this year. The governor says people are owed a legal, constitutional and effective method for carrying out the death penalty.

This is not the first problem this year. In May, another Tennessee execution was halted. Officials have not said where Pike was taken, and it is unclear what will happen next for her.
why_it_matters: It shows how a state is checking its own rules when something goes wrong, and why people ask careful questions about serious punishments.
